bonds_big.h:
THE BIG PICTURE · AS OF NOV 13 CLOSE
Treasuries had their worst week in more than a year: the 10-year closed at 5.15% on Friday, up 29 bp since last Friday, and the 2-year at 4.88%, up 37 bp. Friday added 5 bp after October producer prices rose 6.5% from a year earlier, the most since November 2022, and Boston Fed President Collins said "soon some additional firming" is appropriate. December is about 92% priced and Kalshi's January hike odds rose to 62%.
5.15% 10-yr, Nov 13 close+29 bp since last Friday92% December hike odds
📍 What's happening
  • Yields jumped across the curve this week. Since last Friday the 2-year is up 37 bp to 4.88%, the 10-year 29 bp to 5.15% and the 30-year 21 bp to 5.47%, so the gap between the 2- and 10-year narrowed to 27 bp from 35 bp.
  • Inflation data kept the pressure on. October CPI rose 0.4% and PPI 0.3%, lifting producer prices 6.5% from a year earlier; PPI excluding food, energy and trade rose 0.5%.
  • Hike bets firmed again. Kalshi and Polymarket each priced a December hike at 91.5% (Nov 13, 12:28 PM ET), up from about 77% last Friday; January rose to 62% and March is 62%. Collins said a tighter path than she expected may be needed.
  • Auction demand was soft. The 3-, 10- and 30-year sales all tailed, the first time since May. Stocks still rose for the week, the S&P 500 2.5% and the Nasdaq 2.2%, despite Friday's 0.4% and 0.9% declines.
🏢 What it means for real estate
  • Fixed-rate quotes are rising again. Mortgage News Daily's daily 30-year rose to 7.50% on Nov 13, up 20 bp in two sessions, while Freddie Mac's weekly survey was 7.11% on Nov 12. The 10-year is 97 bp higher this year.
  • Floating-rate debt faces back-to-back hikes. With December about 92% priced and January 62%, SOFR-based bridge and construction loans are likely to reset higher by early 2027, and rate caps cost more.
  • Credit spreads are calm. The high-yield spread was 330 bp on Nov 11, down from 342 bp last Friday, and investment grade 90 bp; lenders still sized a $265M refinancing for the Hilton Boston Park Plaza.
  • Leverage is thinner. Multifamily and industrial cap rates (~5.20%) sit about 5 bp over the 10-year, versus 230–340 bp historically, and Trepp's October CMBS delinquency was 12.33% for office and 8.09% for multifamily.
🧭 Where we think it's headed
Most likely5.00–5.35%

The 10-year stays above 5% into year-end as the Fed hikes in December and markets keep pricing a January follow-up, with producer prices running 6.5% and Brent in the mid-$90s.

Inflation and growth cool4.75–5.00%

Soft October retail sales (Nov 17) or PCE (Nov 25), a renewed drop in oil on progress toward ending the Iran war, or deeper AI-stock losses pull January hike odds back below even.

Hawkish turn5.35–5.60%

A 50 bp December hike, hawkish FOMC minutes (Nov 18), weak demand at the 20-year and TIPS auctions or Brent back above $100 pushes the 10-year past its 5.31% high of Oct 5.

▲ Risks that push yields higher
  1. A larger or longer hiking cycle. December is about 92% priced and January 62%; Collins says a tighter path than she expected may be needed, and Waller has said a half-point move is possible.
  2. Sticky inflation. Producer prices rose 6.5% from a year earlier in October, the most since 2022, and core CPI rose 0.3% for a third straight month.
  3. Oil. Brent was $96.14 on Nov 13 after Trump said the U.S. no longer needs an Iran deal; it was $113.43 on Oct 30.
  4. Soft auction demand and bigger deficits. All three refunding auctions tailed this week, October's deficit was a record $404B, and Treasury expects to borrow $800B in Jan–Mar after $618B in Oct–Dec.
  5. A firm labor market. Jobless claims were 200,000 last week with a four-week average of 195,250, the lowest since 1969, and October payrolls rose 165,000.
  6. Strong growth. Q3 GDP grew 3.4% and ISM manufacturing was 55.5 in October.
▼ Things that could pull yields lower
  1. Cheaper oil. Brent is about $17 below its Oct 30 level and fell 2.2% this week; a lasting end to the U.S.–Iran war would ease fuel and inflation pressure.
  2. An AI-stock unwind. Nvidia's slide deepened on Nov 13 after its CEO stepped down, and the Nasdaq fell 0.9%; it fell 5.5% on Nov 5.
  3. A weakening housing market. October existing-home sales fell 5.5% to a 3.75 million pace, the slowest since 2010, and daily mortgage rates are back at 7.50%.
  4. Cooling wages. Hourly earnings are up 3.1% over the year, and private wage growth slowed to 3.1% in Q3, the least since 2021.

bonds_head.h: Who is borrowing, how much, and at what price: Treasury auctions, jumbo corporate and municipal deals, and credit spreads. Treasuries had their worst week in more than a year: the 10-year closed at 5.15% on Nov 13, up 29 bp since last Friday, and the 2-year at 4.88%, up 37 bp, after a hot October CPI, President Trump's Iran comments, three tailed refunding auctions and, on Friday, a 6.5% annual rise in producer prices. Boston Fed President Collins said more tightening is appropriate soon; December is about 92% priced and Kalshi's January hike odds are 62%. Credit spreads are still calm, with high yield at 330 bp and investment grade at 90 bp on Nov 11. Big Tech borrowing continues after Meta's $15B U.S. sale and €9B euro debut and Apple's $7.5B.

bonds_tsy.h: All three legs of the $125B November refunding drew soft demand, and the 10-year finished the week at 5.15%, up 29 bp since last Friday. Thursday's $25B 30-year stopped at 5.441%, 0.4 bp above the when-issued yield, with a 2.36 bid-to-cover versus 2.54 in October; indirect bidders took 68.1%, directs 20.5% and dealers 11.4%. Tuesday's $42B 10-year cleared at 5.020% with about a 1 bp tail and Monday's $58B 3-year at 4.627% with a 0.5 bp tail. Next week Treasury sells $16B of 20-year bonds on Wed, Nov 18 and $19B of reopened 10-year TIPS on Thu, Nov 19. October's deficit was a record $404B, up 42% from a year earlier. Treasury expects to keep coupon and FRN sizes unchanged "for the next several quarters," plans up to $70B of liquidity buybacks next quarter, and estimates borrowing of $618B for Oct–Dec and $800B for Jan–Mar.

bonds_tsy_note.h: This week's refunding sold into a rising market and demand slipped: the 30-year's 2.36 bid-to-cover was below October's 2.54, indirect bidders took 68.1% versus 72.3%, and it was the first week since May in which the 3-, 10- and 30-year auctions all tailed. The 30-year closed at 5.47% on Nov 13, above the 5.441% auction yield. Next week's $16B 20-year (Nov 18) comes with the 20-year at 5.52%, and the $19B 10-year TIPS reopening (Nov 19) follows a 6.5% annual rise in producer prices, with December about 92% priced and January hike odds at 62%, so weak demand there would add to upward pressure on long rates.

cap_caps.h: Core cap rates by sector against a 10-year that closed at 5.15% on Nov 13, up 29 bp since last Friday. Multifamily and industrial, both at 5.20%, now price only about 5 bp above the 10-year, versus 2010–2020 average spreads of 230 bp and 340 bp; strip retail at 6.40% and office at 7.40% sit about 125 bp and 225 bp above, against historical averages of 320 bp and 280 bp, and hotel at 8.50% is about 335 bp above, with no historical average given. With December about 92% priced and January hike odds at 62%, that cushion is unlikely to widen soon. Recent pricing: the 1,060-room Hilton Boston Park Plaza refinanced with a $265M Athene and Apollo-affiliated loan (about $250,000 per room), LaSalle paid $36M (about $660/SF) for a FedEx-leased truck terminal in Northborough, and 100 Summer St. went at a foreclosure auction for $260M, 68% below its 2019 price.

cap_cmbs.h: CMBS delinquency by property type in August and September (Trepp). Trepp's October report, published Nov 3, shows the overall rate dipping to 7.87% from 8.02% as a large loan returned to current, while office rose 17 bp to 12.33%, multifamily 5 bp to 8.09% and retail 63 bp to 7.21%; lodging fell to 5.94% and industrial to 1.10%. Refinancing got harder this week: the 10-year closed at 5.15% on Nov 13, up 29 bp since last Friday, all three refunding auctions tailed, and December hike odds reached about 92%. Lenders are still active for large assets, with the Hilton Boston Park Plaza refinanced for $265M, while local distress keeps surfacing, including a Dec 8 foreclosure auction for a grocery-anchored Westborough center. Credit spreads stay calm: high yield was 330 bp on Nov 11, down from 342 bp last Friday, and investment grade 90 bp.

cap_cost.h: Building costs are still climbing: the Turner Building Cost Index rose 1.48% in Q3 to 1,575, up 5.49% from a year earlier, and construction input prices were up 11.7% year over year in September, led by diesel (+115.2%), energy (+69.9%) and metals. October producer prices, released Nov 13, rose 0.3% on the month and 6.5% from a year earlier, the most since November 2022, with goods up 0.5%; AGC's October construction breakdown is still to come. A Boston developer told Banker & Tradesman that hard construction costs have risen by more than half and the cost of capital by 20% to 30%, while rents have grown only 1.1%. Financing costs rose again with the 10-year at 5.15%, up 29 bp since last Friday, so replacement costs stay elevated.

cap_fed.h: Markets now price back-to-back hikes: December is about 92% priced, with Kalshi and Polymarket 25 bp contracts each at 91.5% (Nov 13, 12:28 PM ET), up from 89.5% on Nov 12 and about 77% last Friday. Kalshi's January hike odds rose to 62% from 59%, and March is also 62%. Boston Fed President Collins said "soon some additional firming, tightening of policy is appropriate" and that a tighter path than she expected a couple of months ago may be needed, after October producer prices rose 6.5% from a year earlier. Earlier this week Daly, Hammack and Goolsbee also leaned hawkish. The Fed held at 3.75–4.00% on Oct 28 with two dissents for a hike; it meets Dec 8–9.

cap_fed_note.h: Odds are a snapshot from Nov 13, 12:28 PM ET via DeFi Rate. December's 25 bp hike contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket both traded at 91.5%, up from 89.5% on Nov 12; DeFi Rate's meeting table shows a higher 97% for December, so treat the figures as approximate. January hike odds rose to 62% from 59%, and March is 62%, up from 61%. Next: October retail sales on Nov 17 at 8:30 AM, FOMC minutes on Nov 18 at 2:00 PM, and October PCE on Nov 25.

cap_fuel.h: Oil held near Thursday's rebound: Brent edged up 0.3% to $96.14 on Friday but finished the week down 2.2% from $98.32 last Friday, after President Trump said the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Iran; it was $113.43 on Oct 30. October producer prices showed energy down 0.1% on the month after a 10.8% jump in September, while consumer energy prices rose 0.7%. EIA has not posted weekly pump prices since Oct 26, when U.S. diesel was $6.352 (+$2.634 from a year ago), New England diesel $6.421 and Boston gasoline $4.176. Diesel feeds construction, trucking and heating costs (diesel producer prices were up 115.2% in September), so crude in the mid-$90s keeps winter operating budgets elevated.

cap_opex.h: Energy is the swing factor for winter budgets: Brent was $96.14 on Nov 13 (from $113.43 on Oct 30), EIA's latest New England diesel price was still $6.421 (Oct 26), winter heating oil costs are projected up 31% per household, and Eversource NH's winter rate is 17.32¢ per kWh (up 10%). October CPI rose 0.4%, with shelter up 0.3% and energy 0.7%, and producer prices rose 6.5% from a year earlier, so vendor and service contracts are still repricing higher. Property insurance is getting cheaper: commercial property premiums fell 6.3% in Q2, the fourth straight quarterly decline, though umbrella liability rose 5.3%. Labor costs are firm: hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the year in October, jobless claims are near 200,000, and employer health insurance costs rose 6.4% over the year in Q3.

cap_rates.h: Treasury curve over the past year. The 10-year closed at 5.15% on Friday, Nov 13, up 29 bp since last Friday, its biggest weekly rise in more than a year. It added 5 bp on Friday, touching 5.17% intraday, after October producer prices rose 6.5% from a year earlier, the most since November 2022, and Boston Fed President Collins said more tightening is appropriate soon. Since last Friday the 2-year is up 37 bp to 4.88%, its highest close since Sep 30, and the 30-year 21 bp to 5.47%, so the 2- to 10-year gap narrowed to 27 bp from 35 bp. The 10-year matched its Oct 19 close, is 16 bp below its 52-week high of 5.31% on Oct 5 and is 97 bp higher this year; the Fed holds at 3.75–4.00%.

cap_supply.h: Pipelines are shrinking in most Sun Belt metros, with 2026 deliveries projected down 47% in Austin, 40% in Phoenix and more than half in Denver, while Nashville completions are down 41%. Miami's pipeline is still expanding (above 8% of inventory) and Charlotte's is among the highest in the U.S. (above 8%). Boston has 14,523 units in its pipeline and vacancy at 5.6%, but private development is stalling: approvals fell to 7,746 units, the fewest in at least a decade, the region added just 9,000 residents in 2025, and the approved 754-unit Morrissey Boulevard project in Dorchester is tied up in a dispute after a $67.5M sale failed to close. Subsidized and conversion projects are still getting financed, including $48M for 116 senior units in Danvers and $9.3M for a 58-unit mill conversion in Worcester. For-sale housing is stuck, with October existing-home sales at their slowest pace since 2010 and daily mortgage rates at 7.50%, which keeps more households renting. Boston rents are still rising but cooling into winter: Zumper's October 1-bedroom median was $2,980 (+2.8% YoY, −0.7% on the month), Zillow's September metro rent $2,987 (+2.3%) and Apartment List's October metro median $2,233 (+1.0%).

con_head.h: Households are running on a thinner cushion: the saving rate fell to 3.8% in September 2026, the lowest since 2022, and Michigan sentiment ended October at 48.0, near record lows, while median wage growth held at 3.9% in September and bank card delinquency eased to 2.85% in Q2. Spending is still holding up, with real retail sales up 2.5% from a year earlier in September, which favors grocery, value and off-price tenants and argues for watching collections from lower-income renters.

mig_fc.h: Nationally, 227,548 foreclosure filings were recorded in H1 2026, 0.16% of housing units and up 21.26% from a year earlier. Bank repossessions (REO) reached 27,983, up 33%, and foreclosure starts were 164,566, up 18%. The latest monthly figure available here, for August, was 40,277 filings, up 1% from the prior month and 13% from a year earlier. Florida (0.27%), South Carolina (0.26%), Delaware and Indiana (0.25%) and Illinois (0.23%) had the highest state rates in H1. Massachusetts had 2,719 filings, a rate of 0.09% (one in 1,115 units), up 3.23% from a year earlier; New Hampshire had 488, a rate of 0.08% (one in 1,329 units), up 23.54%. Both rates are well below the national rate. ATTOM's Q3 and September foreclosure reports were not found as of Nov 13.
